overview: This map record covers Kashmir around 700 to 800 CE, during the Karkota dynasty. Its rulers supported temples, monasteries and learned communities. The imported outline is approximate, not a surveyed frontier or a statement about modern sovereignty. The dynasty continued beyond the map’s endpoint.

periods.title: Karkota beginnings
periods.summary: Durlabhavardhana established the dynasty in the seventh century; early dates remain approximate.

periods.title: The mapped century
periods.summary: Lalitaditya’s building patronage belongs to this period of Karkota rule.

periods.title: After the map
periods.summary: Karkota rule continued into the ninth century before Utpala succession.

sections.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work

items.text: Much of the royal story comes from Kalhana, writing around 1149 to 1150. His chronicle preserves earlier dynastic information, but he lived centuries after the Karkotas. Historians compare its chronology with outside records instead of treating every royal story as an eyewitness report.

Kalhana associates Lalitaditya’s religious foundations with grants of villages to Brahmins. Royal patronage connected temples with landed resources, making control of the countryside part of the story too.

Parihasapura, founded by Lalitaditya in the eighth century, contained Buddhist and Hindu monuments. Surviving remains include a stupa, a monastery and Vishnu temples. Its builders worked with enormous stone blocks: creating a royal religious center required organized labor as well as impressive royal ambitions.

Excavation at Parihasapura in 1914 exposed buildings beneath the ruined site. Archaeology lets a visitor compare the physical remains with written accounts: platforms, blocks and building plans survive even when the original roofs and many images have disappeared.

Martand was a sanctuary of Surya, the sun god. Its surviving courtyard and carved stonework still make the building’s scale visible. Looking at a temple means looking at the work of people who quarried, shaped and fitted the stone, as well as the deity honored there.

Even coins can be historical puzzles. Numismatist John Deyell questioned the traditional attribution of some gold-alloy coins to Kashmir’s Karkota rulers: their find locations and several royal names do not fit comfortably. A familiar museum label can be a research question rather than the final answer.

The Nilamata Purana preserves rituals associated with Kashmir. Its editor Ved Kumari Ghai dates the core broadly to the sixth through eighth centuries, with later additions. Its festival instructions reveal household ideals, rather than proving that every family celebrated identically.

For snowfall celebrations, the Nilamata recommends substantial cloaks, special food and gathering on the snow with children, relatives, friends and servants. Music accompanies the meal. Apparently a winter picnic required both a good guest list and very warm clothes.

Another celebration calls for lamps at houses, shops, crossroads and rivers, with cloth decorating the shops. Friends, relatives and servants share a meal after sunset. The same text exempts children and sick people from that day’s fasting requirement.

Written-language sample: नमस्ते नागराजेन्द्र means “Salutation to you, sovereign-king of the Nagas.” This Sanskrit greeting opens a hymn to Nila, the serpent king. It is shown in modern Devanagari transcription of the transmitted text, not copied from an eighth-century inscription.

A Kashmir Buddha figure dated around 800 stands only 14.6 centimeters high. Its maker combined brass with silver and copper inlays; a forehead setting once held a gemstone. The sculpture represents the infant Buddha with several adult attributes, including curled hair and elongated earlobes.

The same figure carries a donor’s message in Kashmir’s Sharada script. The museum translates its opening as “This is the pious gift of Shrideva,” but the donor’s following description is uncertain. That small inscription preserves a person’s name and an act of generosity across twelve centuries.

An eighth-century ivory carving from Kashmir fits a dancer and two musicians into a piece about 4.5 centimeters wide. One musician plays a drum hanging from his shoulders; the other holds what the curator tentatively identifies as a tambourine. Tiny does not mean simple.

Traces of color remain on that ivory. The curator suggests it belonged to a portable shrine and may portray a Buddhist story involving Mara’s daughter. Its music-making figures are therefore evidence of artistic imagination and familiar instruments, rather than a labeled photograph of an ordinary party.

Another eighth-century Kashmir ivory shows the Buddha descending three steps after teaching his mother in heaven. At just 6.4 centimeters high, it turns a story about a son and his mother into something small enough to carry. Attendants hold ceremonial accessories beside him.

A late eighth-century stone Vishnu has four faces: a human face, a lion, a boar, and a fierce face carved behind the halo. You have to look around the sculpture to discover the fourth. This form was especially important in Kashmir’s religious art.

The Vishnu sculpture also turns equipment into characters. Its original attendants personified the god’s discus and mace; the mace figure is now missing. The earth goddess appears between his legs. The sculptor packed divine relationships into a single stone image about a meter tall.

ending.text: The map ends at 800, but the Karkota dynasty did not. Utpala rulers succeeded it around the middle of the ninth century. Kashmir’s religious, literary and artistic communities continued through that political change.
